title: Fayum mummy portraits
summary: Realistic funerary portraits, often painted on wood in the encaustic technique, became very popular in Roman-ruled Egypt in the first through third centuries AD. Many come from cemeteries such as Hawara in the Fayum, where Flinders Petrie found some 60 panels. They blend Egyptian, Greek and Roman customs.

uncertainty.note: Getty gives the first through third centuries AD; National Geographic describes the wider Egyptian-Greek-Roman cultural mixing as running from the first century B.C. through the fourth century A.D. Range here follows the Getty wording for the portraits themselves.

as_recorded.value: In the first through third centuries AD, a new form of funerary artifact—the mummy portrait—became very popular in Egypt
from the first century B.C. through to the fourth century A.D.

where.modern_name: Hawara necropolis, Faiyum Governorate, Egypt (largest group; portraits also found at other sites)

importance.justification: Widely known surviving portraits of ordinary individuals in Roman Egypt that show a fusion of Egyptian funerary practice with Greek and Roman art.
